clips.send: A friend bragging about intermittent fasting sends it to themselves first - the anxious thought they might be on a modified diet, not a real fast.
clips.caption:
Dr. Daniel Pompa told Kevin Trudeau that most people doing 'intermittent fasting' today aren't actually fasting at all.

His point: a real fast is water, maybe an herbal tea - nothing else. The juice fast, the liquid diet, the shortened eating window people call fasting now are modified versions, not the real thing.

His push: know which one you're actually doing before you count on the benefits of the other.

Which kind of 'fast' have you actually been doing?

clips.send: A caregiver nursing someone through a health scare sends it for the hope in Dr. Pompa's story - the fear a hospital IV could make things worse, and the awe that the body knew when to drink again.
clips.caption:
Dr. Daniel Pompa told Kevin Trudeau about a client who nearly died, then went 12 days with no food or water at all.

His point: the man's body told him exactly when it was safe to drink again - and he knew, without being told, when it was time to eat. It took about 23 days before food came back into the picture.

His lesson: the body has its own intelligence, reading hunger and thirst as real signals, not just habit.

Would you trust your body to tell you when?

clips.send: Someone on a daily prescription sends it to their spouse before the next refill - the anger of learning pharma drugs may out-kill the diseases they treat, and the fear of what else they weren't told.
clips.caption:
Dr. Daniel Pompa told Kevin Trudeau a number most people never hear.

His source: the former director of the FDA, who told Kevin while he was writing his own book that more people die from pharmaceutical drugs than from the diseases those drugs are prescribed for.

His one caution: never stop a medication on your own. His real point is simpler - ask your doctor what else could be driving the problem before adding another pill.

Have you ever asked your doctor that question?

clips.send: Someone just put on a statin sends it to their doctor before the next appointment - the anger of a shifting 'normal' number, and the anxiety that the number, not their health, decided it.
clips.caption:
Dr. Daniel Pompa told Kevin Trudeau why the cholesterol number keeps moving.

His point: 'normal' cholesterol was once 350, then 300, then 250 - now anything over 200 can land you on a medication. He points to the Cochrane Collaboration, a group that reviews large batches of studies, which found little link between cholesterol and heart attacks.

His view: a number that keeps shifting lower is worth a second look before you accept it.

Has your own 'normal' number ever changed on you?
